title: Trust Recovery
concept: Proof items, for a real breach: the one who broke trust names it, you agree one change you can both see, and you look at the record together at each check back, feelings first.
whenToUse: After a betrayal, a lie or a string of broken agreements, or anything that leaves a clear before and after in how safe things feel. A breach is something the partner agrees they did. Seeing friends or family, privacy or a locked phone is never a breach. You cannot be made to accept a breach you do not agree happened. Steps 2 to 5 also work alone, as a Proof item, when a request for change meets only “I promise”.
steps: Name what happened, clearly, without deflecting. The partner who broke trust names it and acknowledges the impact; the hurt partner is never asked to confess in return.
Decide on one specific change you can both see. Any transparency is offered voluntarily by the partner who broke trust, for a set time, and never becomes monitoring.

Set a time window, two to four weeks to start (1 to 2 weeks for a smaller Proof item). Extending it takes both of you. Put the check-back dates in the calendar. Either of you can end it at a check back.
Keep a simple table of facts only, and look at it together. Anything about someone’s pauses is noted only if the one pausing agrees.
Check back: the hurt partner’s feelings and questions come first. The record is an aid, never the judge. Then decide together to keep going, change it, or call it done.
If it’s not safe, stop and get outside support.

phrases.text: What happened was ___. I’m not debating that.
My proof: ___. You’ll see it when ___.
Looking at the record: met, partial or missed.

working: B names what happened, the drinks with a colleague kept quiet, and makes no excuses. The proof: B ends the private chats and says so at each weekly check back. They meet weekly for four weeks, A’s feelings first. One week is only partly kept and B owns it. A says it’s helping, so they carry on.
notWorking: Week two, B skips the heads-up and offers another long apology: “Can’t you just trust me again?” Or A pulls out the record mid-row to shame B. Demanding passwords, tracking location or reading messages isn’t proof; it’s monitoring.
activity: Fill in one Proof row and the four-week table together.
warn: If it’s not safe, stop and get outside support. Transparency is offered voluntarily, is time-limited, and never becomes monitoring: no demanding passwords, tracking location or reading messages. If refusing the “voluntary” transparency would feel unsafe, it isn’t voluntary: stop and use the Help Lines. If you can’t agree that a breach happened, this tool isn’t for it: get outside support.
note: Deciding not to rebuild, or to end the relationship, is a valid outcome of this tool, not a failure of it.
